name: Affirmations / self-talk

image.caption: 130424 Image of Positive Mindset Affirmations on Making a Difference

lead: Affirmations are positive statements people repeat or write to change how they see themselves, often used to counter negative face or body image. The payoff is a softer self-image and a more relaxed, confident presence.

Self-affirmation theory, proposed by Claude Steele in 1988, holds that reflecting on valued domains protects overall self-worth and reduces defensiveness under threat; it has produced experimental findings on stress. Repeating positive statements is a separate practice: a 2009 study by Wood and colleagues found present-tense statements such as 'I am...' helped people with high self-esteem but left those with low self-esteem feeling worse. No studies have tested affirmations for appearance outcomes.

paras: People repeat or write statements daily, often in the morning or in front of a mirror, in present tense and personalised to them. Some choose value-based reflection, writing about what matters to them, instead of statements about looks.
No physical risks are documented. Studies suggest present-tense positive statements may worsen mood for people with low self-esteem.

angle.text: Users repeat positive statements to counter negative face or body image, aiming for a softer self-image and a more relaxed, confident presence. Value-based self-affirmation has research on stress and defensiveness; affirmations for looks have not been tested.

lead: Affirmations and self-talk are mental practices in which a person repeats, writes or silently says encouraging statements, or reflects on personal values, to change how they see and speak to themselves. In looks-related use, people apply them to quiet harsh judgments of their face and body, aiming for steadier confidence that shows up as more upright posture, easier eye contact and a calmer social presence, and for the consistency that keeps training, skincare and grooming routines going.[1][2][3]

Two separate traditions sit under the same name. Positive affirmations come from the New Thought and self-help movement, running from Wallace Wattles' 1910 book The Science of Getting Rich through Louise Hay's 1984 You Can Heal Your Life to Rhonda Byrne's 2006 The Secret.[1] Self-affirmation theory is an academic framework proposed by the social psychologist Claude Steele in 1988, in which people reflect on important values to protect their sense of self-worth under threat.[2][4] A third body of work, from sport psychology, studies the instructional and motivational phrases athletes say to themselves.[5][6]

Research on each strand exists, but none has measured facial or physical appearance as an outcome. Studies describe lower stress responses and less defensiveness after value-based self-affirmation,[2][4] a moderate performance benefit from sport self-talk,[5] and a 2009 finding by Wood and colleagues that repeating present-tense positive statements helped people with high self-esteem and left people with low self-esteem feeling worse.[7] Lifters on forums such as T Nation describe self-talk mainly as a way to get through demanding sessions.[8][9]

paras: In the New Thought and New Age sense, an affirmation is a carefully worded statement repeated aloud or silently and often written down. Teachers commonly describe effective ones as present tense, positive, personal and specific.[1] Practitioners also use affirming images, words and videos, classes and lectures, mantra chanting, and hypnosis; the practice appears in neuro-linguistic programming and in the 'neuro-associative conditioning' popularised by Anthony Robbins.[1]

Wikipedia traces the modern movement through Wallace Wattles' 1910 The Science of Getting Rich, which inspired Rhonda Byrne, and through Napoleon Hill's Think and Grow Rich, which expresses similar ideas.[1] Louise Hay, a Religious Science practitioner, published You Can Heal Your Life in 1984; her affirmations aim to replace beliefs she thought supported illness with beliefs she thought supported healing.[1] Byrne's 2006 book and film The Secret brought the idea of the law of attraction to a mass audience.[1] The belief behind these traditions is summed up in the article as a conviction that a positive mental attitude supported by affirmations will achieve success in anything.[1]

Some teachers add conditions. Esther Hicks, author of the Law of Attraction books, recommends using affirmations when one is already happy and at peace, and Rhonda Britten suggests pairing them with 'acknowledgements', records of steps already taken, so that attention goes to progress rather than self-criticism. Her example is noting the purchase of gym clothes in support of a weight-loss goal.[1]

Self-affirmation theory was popularised by Claude Steele in the late 1980s, building on his 1988 chapter 'The Psychology of Self-Affirmation'. Its central idea is that people are motivated to protect their self-integrity, a sense of being good, adequate and moral, and that a threat in one area can be offset by affirming a strength in another.[2] Sherman and Cohen's 2006 review extended the framework.[2]

In experiments, participants typically rank values such as aesthetic, social, political, religious, economic and theoretical, and then write for about five minutes on a top-ranked value, or complete a values scale.[2] Cohen and Sherman's 2014 Annual Review of Psychology article describes the technique as writing about core personal values, which produces a more expansive view of the self and weakens the implications of a threat; the authors report benefits for education, health and relationships that sometimes persist for months or years.[4]

Reported findings include lower cortisol responses to a laboratory stressor (Creswell and colleagues, 2005), equal problem-solving performance for high-stress and low-stress students after affirmation (Creswell, 2013), and greater acceptance of a health-risk article among heavy coffee drinkers, for whom the threat was personal (Sherman, Nelson and Steele, 2000).[2] Cohen and colleagues' school studies (2006, 2009) reported higher grades among affirmed minority seventh-graders over two years, and Logel and Cohen (2012) reported that weight-concerned women who completed a values essay lost more weight and had lower BMI and smaller waist circumference.[2]

Wikipedia notes limits and open questions: the mechanism has not been identified; results on mood and self-esteem are mixed; effects vary across cultures, with Heine and Lehman (1997) finding reduced dissonance for individualist but not collectivist participants; many studies use undergraduates; benefits appear mainly when the threatened domain matters to the person; and the stress findings are described as preliminary.[2] A pilot trial in end-stage renal disease reported better phosphate control after affirmation.[2]

sections.h: Positive self-statements and the 'I am' format
paras: The best-known test of repeated present-tense statements is Wood, Perunovic and Lee's 2009 paper in Psychological Science. A survey found that people often use positive self-statements and believe they work. In two experiments, participants with low self-esteem who repeated a statement such as 'I am a lovable person' felt worse than those who did not, as did those who dwelt on how the statement was true, while participants with high self-esteem felt somewhat better. The authors concluded the statements may help some people but may backfire for those who most need them.[7] Wikipedia adds that people with low self-esteem fared better with statements that allowed for doubt or were future-tense, such as 'I will'.[1]

Later work has looked at brain responses and combinations with other methods. Wikipedia reports a 2016 fMRI study by Cascio and colleagues in which self-affirmation engaged reward-related regions (the ventral striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex) and future-oriented affirmations were linked to objectively measured behaviour change, and a 2024 paper associating affirmative practices combined with mindfulness with better emotional self-regulation.[1] A 2024 fMRI study of 21 adults found that hearing self-affirmation statements in one's own voice versus another voice engaged different brain regions, with greater precuneus involvement for the own-voice version.[10] A 2025 psychology paper examined belief in manifestation, the idea behind The Secret.[11]

Wikipedia distinguishes self-talk, a single voice addressing itself, from inner dialogue, in which several voices take turns. It describes instructional self-talk, which directs attention to the components of a task and can help while a physical skill is being learned but may hurt people already skilled at it, and coping self-talk, which emphasises strengths and skills without implying perfection and can help people calm down and set realistic goals.[12] Second-person ('you') phrasing is used more when people regulate themselves or face difficult actions, and in one study cited there second-person suggestions were more effective than other forms for promoting intentions to act.[12]

In cognitive behavioural therapy, negative core beliefs are thought to drive negative self-talk, and a key method is to notice these beliefs and question whether they are true. Mindfulness is a related approach that encourages evaluating experiences without judgment.[12]

Distanced self-talk is a research variant. A set of seven studies (585 participants) published in 2014 found that using one's own name or non-first-person pronouns during introspection improved thoughts, feelings and behaviour under social stress, including in socially anxious people.[13] A 2022 Scientific Reports paper reported that distanced self-talk increased rational self-interest in decision tasks.[14]

Sport psychology has measured self-talk directly. A meta-analysis of 32 studies (62 effect sizes) found a positive, moderate effect of self-talk on sport task performance.[5] A systematic review of 47 studies reported beneficial effects of positive, instructional and motivational self-talk, while also noting that negative self-talk did not impede performance in the studies analysed and that evidence for different effects of instructional versus motivational self-talk was inconsistent.[6] A 2005 study quantified the self-talk of athletes during competition.[15]

In a randomised between-group trial of endurance cycling, motivational self-talk reduced perceived effort and extended time to exhaustion.[16] The Wikipedia article on self-talk observes that sport psychology widely assumes positive self-talk helps and negative self-talk hinders, with some empirical support but not thorough research.[12]

Lifters describe the same practice in training logs. One T Nation poster wrote of a hard workout with 'lots of self-talk', said out loud, to get through all the work.[8] Another mentioned self-talk while pushing through sprints and a martial arts class that was a hard sell to himself.[9] A T Nation thread quotes a piece attributed to Brandon Webb on the importance of self-talk, framing it as a core training skill rather than 'airy-fairy' personal-growth talk.[17] The training chain is straightforward: sessions completed, then more total work, then physique change over months.

sections.h: How people use it for looks
paras: People who link affirmations to appearance describe a behavioural and presentational route rather than a change in facial or bodily structure. They report less self-criticism before social situations, more upright posture and steadier eye contact, and better follow-through on training, skincare and grooming routines. These reports are descriptions of what practitioners say, not measured outcomes.

The closest research concerns appearance-linked behaviour. Randomised trials have tested self-affirmation approaches for sun protection and for reducing defensiveness toward health-risk messages,[18][19] and Logel and Cohen's weight study is described on Wikipedia.[2] Distanced self-talk, tested under social stress in the 2014 studies, is the research variant most relevant to confidence in social situations.[13]

Wikipedia's article on body image links poor body image with lower self-esteem and with attempts to change the body through dieting or cosmetic surgery, and describes interventions such as school body-confidence lessons and body-positive media.[3] Studies of affirmation in this area have given mixed results. In a 2026 experiment with 250 college-aged women, viewing idealised influencer posts lowered body satisfaction and positive affect, and neither general nor body-positive self-affirmation writing tasks protected against the effect; the body-positive task may have worsened it.[20]

A 2025 randomised trial of 158 young Japanese women found that a combined intervention reducing the negative facet of self-compassion and increasing the positive facet reduced body dissatisfaction and improved self-esteem compared with control, a result related to, but distinct from, affirmation.[21] Self-compassion, mindfulness and cognitive-behavioural methods are the neighbouring practices that body-image researchers more often test.

No studies found testing affirmations for physical appearance outcomes. Related randomised trials and reviews cover self-affirmation for stress, performance and health behaviour,[4][18][19] self-talk for sport performance,[5][16][6] and the 2009 and 2026 experiments on positive statements and body satisfaction described above.[7][20]

lore.intro: In training and self-improvement forums, affirmations and self-talk come up as a mindset tool, usually in terms of motivation, discipline and confidence rather than facial structure.[22][8][9]

Louise Hay publishes You Can Heal Your Life.[1]
Claude Steele advances self-affirmation theory in 'The Psychology of Self-Affirmation'.[2]
Heine and Lehman report that affirmation reduced dissonance for individualist but not collectivist participants.[2]
Sherman, Nelson and Steele report greater acceptance of a health-risk article after affirmation.[2]
Creswell and colleagues report lower cortisol responses to a laboratory stressor after values affirmation.[2]
Rhonda Byrne's The Secret released as a film and book; Cohen and colleagues begin reporting school affirmation results.[1][2]
Wood, Perunovic and Lee report that positive self-statements helped high-self-esteem participants and worsened mood for low-self-esteem participants.[7]
Logel and Cohen report greater weight loss among affirmed weight-concerned women.[2]
Cohen and Sherman review self-affirmation interventions; seven studies of distanced self-talk are published.[4][13]
Cascio and colleagues report an fMRI study of self-affirmation.[1]
Experiment finds self-affirmation tasks did not protect body satisfaction after idealised Instagram content.[20]
